title: THE SERPENT BRUISED HIS HEEL… BUT HE NEVER SAW HIS OWN HEAD ABOUT TO BE CRUSHED
paragraphs: THE SERPENT BRUISED HIS HEEL… BUT HE NEVER SAW HIS OWN HEAD ABOUT TO BE CRUSHED

The first promise of Jesus Christ was spoken in the middle of humanity’s greatest scandal. Before the nails, before the crown of thorns, before the empty tomb, God had already announced that the serpent’s victory would become his defeat. And buried inside that ancient promise is a truth that could change the way you see your sin, your suffering, your battles, and the Savior who refused to abandon you.
There was a moment in human history when everything beautiful broke.
No armies marched. No cities burned. No nails pierced a Savior’s hands.
There was only a garden.
A man. A woman. A serpent.
And a question that sounded innocent enough to destroy the world.
“Yea, hath God said…?” (Genesis 3:1, KJV).
That was how the serpent began.
Not with a sword.
With suspicion.
He did not need to convince Eve that God did not exist. He only needed her to question whether God could be trusted.
And isn't that still how so many of our darkest battles begin?
A quiet thought that God is withholding something good. A temptation that promises relief. A compromise that seems harmless. A secret decision nobody else will ever know about.
Until everything changes.
Adam and Eve ate the forbidden fruit.
Their eyes were opened.
But instead of becoming what the serpent had promised, they discovered something terrifying.
They were naked.
They were ashamed.
And for the first time, the people who had walked in fellowship with God wanted to hide from Him.
Imagine that.
The hands that had never trembled with guilt were suddenly reaching for leaves to cover their shame.
The hearts that had known no fear were now racing at the sound of their Creator approaching.
And when God called, “Where art thou?” (Genesis 3:9), Adam did not run toward the voice that had given him life.
He hid.
That is the tragedy of sin.
It does not merely lead us into disobedience.
It teaches us to fear the very God whose presence we were created to enjoy.
Maybe you know something about that.
Maybe you still pray, but there are things you cannot bring yourself to confess.
Maybe you worship on Sunday while carrying a secret you hope nobody discovers on Monday.
Maybe people see your Bible verses, your church attendance, your smiling photographs, and your encouraging words.
But they do not see what happens when the room becomes quiet.
The regret.
The temptation.
The memories.
The private battles.
The shame that whispers, If they knew everything about you, they would never look at you the same way again.
And perhaps the most painful thought of all:
How could God still want someone like me?
If that question has ever kept you awake at night, you need to hear what happened next in Eden.
Because before Adam and Eve could repair anything, before they could offer a sacrifice, before they could prove that they deserved another opportunity, God spoke a promise.
Not first to Adam.
Not first to Eve.
But to the serpent.
And that promise would eventually lead to a bloodstained cross outside Jerusalem.
Genesis 3:15 records these words:
“And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel.” (KJV)
Read those words again.
The serpent would strike.
But the serpent would not have the final victory.
Hidden in the judgment pronounced in Eden was the first announcement of a conflict that would reach its decisive turning point at Calvary.
Christian theology has long called this verse the protoevangelium, a Latin term meaning “first gospel.”
It is the first glimpse of the good news within the unfolding biblical story.
And to understand how astonishing that is, we need to look carefully at what the Hebrew actually says.
The Hebrew text of Genesis 3:15 includes this extraordinary declaration:
הוּא יְשׁוּפְךָ רֹאשׁ וְאַתָּה תְּשׁוּפֶנּוּ עָקֵב
Hu yeshufkha rosh, ve'attah teshufennu aqev.
A close translation is:
“He will strike you at the head, and you will strike him at the heel.”
The Hebrew verb שׁוּף (shuf) is used for both actions. Depending on its context, it can convey striking, bruising, or crushing.
That matters.
Because some Christians have heard this passage explained as though the original Hebrew uses two completely different verbs, one for a minor injury and another for a fatal blow.
It does not.
The same verb appears in both clauses.
The contrast is found especially in the location of the blows.
The head.
And the heel.
A serpent striking a heel can cause terrible injury, even death.
A blow to a serpent’s head, however, points toward the destruction of its power.

The ancient Greek Septuagint renders the decisive clause with language meaning that he will watch for or strike at the serpent’s head, while the serpent will watch for or strike at his heel. This reminds us not to build the entire doctrine on a single English word.
The victory is understood through the whole testimony of Scripture.
And that testimony leads us to Jesus Christ.
But notice something else.
Genesis 3:15 speaks of the woman’s “seed,” or offspring.
The Hebrew word זֶרַע (zeraʿ) can refer collectively to descendants or to an individual descendant, depending on context.
The verse begins with hostility between two lines of offspring, yet its language also allows the reader to focus on a particular representative.
Genesis itself does not yet identify that descendant by name.
The promise unfolds through the rest of the Bible.
Through Abraham.
Through Judah.
Through David.
Through the prophets.
Until, in the fullness of time, a child is born in Bethlehem.
Jesus Christ.
The Son of God.
Born of a woman (Galatians 4:4).
The promised Messiah.
The One who came not merely to improve human behavior, but to confront the ruin sin had brought into the world.
Think about the wonder of that.
The first humans had fallen.
The garden had been corrupted.
The relationship had been broken.
And before the story had even left Eden, God had already revealed that evil would face an enemy it could not ultimately overcome.
Humanity had rebelled.
Yet God was not finished with humanity.
That does not mean sin was harmless.
It does not mean judgment disappeared.
Adam and Eve were expelled from Eden. Suffering and death entered the human story. The consequences of their rebellion were real.
But judgment was not the only word spoken that day.
There was also promise.
And that promise was greater than Adam and Eve could possibly have understood.
Centuries passed.
Generations were born and buried.
Kingdoms rose and collapsed.
God’s people repeatedly wandered into idolatry, injustice, unbelief, and rebellion.
Still, the promise continued.
Then one night, in the humility of Bethlehem, the promised Redeemer entered the world.
Not with the appearance of an earthly conqueror.
But as a baby laid in a manger.
The One through whom all things were made had taken on human flesh.
The eternal Son had entered the very world wounded by human rebellion.
And from the beginning, His earthly life was marked by opposition.
Herod sought to destroy Him.
Satan tempted Him in the wilderness.
Religious leaders plotted against Him.
His own disciple betrayed Him.
His friends abandoned Him.
And eventually, the crowds that had heard His teaching and witnessed His works would see Him condemned to death.
It looked as though darkness was winning.
But darkness had misunderstood the mission of Jesus.
He had not come to avoid suffering at all costs.
He had come to save sinners through His obedient life, sacrificial death, and victorious resurrection.
Listen to the words of 1 John 3:8:
“For this purpose the Son of God was manifested, that he might destroy the works of the devil.” (KJV)
Not negotiate with them.
Not surrender to them.
Destroy them.
And Hebrews 2:14 explains that through death, Christ would destroy the devil’s power over death.
Through death.
Do you see the astonishing reversal?
The very weapon that appeared to secure Satan’s victory became the means by which Christ accomplished redemption.
The cross was not an interruption of God's saving purpose.
It was central to that purpose.
Now imagine Jerusalem.
The morning air heavy with dust.
Roman soldiers moving through the streets.
A crowd gathering around a condemned man.
His back torn by scourging.
His face disfigured by violence.
A crown of thorns pressed into His head.
The hands that had touched lepers and restored the broken were about to be fastened to wood.
The feet that had walked toward the rejected and the forgotten were about to be pierced.
And the Son of God would hang between criminals.
To the watching world, it looked like humiliation.
To His enemies, it looked like defeat.
To His frightened disciples, it looked like the end of everything they had hoped for.
But Scripture reveals something the crowd could not see.
The suffering of Jesus was not merely the cruelty of men.
It was also the fulfillment of God's redemptive purpose.
Isaiah had foretold:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.” (Isaiah 53:5, KJV)
And Peter would later write:
Jesus was not suffering for His own sins.
He had none.
He was bearing the sins of others.
Our pride.
Our rebellion.
Our dishonesty.
Our lust.
Our selfishness.
Our bitterness.
Our refusal to trust God.
Every sin that we are tempted to minimize was serious enough that our redemption required the death of the sinless Son of God.
That truth should humble us.
Because the cross tells us something about sin that our culture rarely wants to admit.
Sin is not merely a mistake.
It is rebellion against a holy God.
And yet the same cross tells us something about divine love that shame struggles to believe.
God did not wait for sinners to make themselves worthy before sending His Son.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had cleaned up every secret.
Not after we had mastered every temptation.
Not after we had repaired every broken relationship.
Christ died for sinners.
This does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes repentance possible without pretending that we can save ourselves.
And then came the moment.
Jesus cried out:
“It is finished.” (John 19:30, KJV)
The Greek word recorded in John's Gospel is τετέλεσται (tetelestai).
It comes from the verb teleō, meaning to finish, accomplish, or bring something to completion.
It is a perfect-tense form, expressing an action brought to completion with an abiding result.
The word itself does not automatically mean “paid in full” in every context, even though related forms could appear in financial settings.
Here, its meaning is anchored in the mission Jesus had come to accomplish.
He had completed the work entrusted to Him.
His obedient sacrifice was not a failed rescue attempt.
It was the fulfillment of His saving mission.
John tells us that after saying these words, Jesus bowed His head and gave up His spirit.
The soldiers saw a dead man.
The disciples faced overwhelming grief.
His body was placed in a tomb.
A stone was rolled across the entrance.
And silence settled over Jerusalem.
But the serpent had not won.
Because on the third day, the tomb was empty.
Jesus Christ rose bodily from the dead.
Death could not hold Him.
The grave could not keep Him.
And the resurrection publicly vindicated the One who had been condemned.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 15:54–57 that death is swallowed up in victory and that God gives us victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.
The resurrection is not simply an inspirational ending to a tragic story.
It is God's declaration that the crucified Jesus is the victorious Lord.
The heel had been struck.
But the promised victory belonged to Christ.
Colossians 2:14–15 describes how Christ dealt with the record of debt against us and triumphed over the hostile powers through the cross.
And Romans 16:20 gives believers an extraordinary promise:
“And the God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly.” (KJV)
There is the language of Genesis again.
The serpent.
The crushing.
The victory.
Only now the people of God are included in the triumph of their Lord.
Not because believers possess independent power over Satan.
Not because Christians are incapable of being tempted.
Not because the battle against evil has already disappeared from our daily experience.
But because the risen Christ has secured the decisive victory, and those who belong to Him will share in its final fulfillment.
Revelation 20:10 looks ahead to the ultimate judgment of the devil.
The enemy's final defeat is certain in the biblical story.
Yet until that final judgment, Christians still live in a world where temptation, suffering, persecution, and death remain painfully real.
That is why this promise matters so deeply.
Because perhaps you are reading this while facing something you thought you would have overcome by now.
Maybe you have repented of the same sin more times than you can count.
Maybe your marriage is strained.
Maybe your family is broken.
Maybe you have buried someone you love, and the silence of their absence feels unbearable.
Maybe you have served in church while secretly wondering why your own heart feels so far from God.
Or maybe your greatest battle is the voice that keeps telling you your past has permanently disqualified you from being loved.
Hear this carefully.
The victory of Jesus does not mean your wounds are imaginary. It means your wounds do not have the authority to overturn His promises.
You may still need to confess what you have hidden.
You may still need to seek forgiveness from someone you have hurt.
You may need to walk away from a relationship that keeps drawing you into sin.
You may need pastoral counsel, accountability, professional help, or the patient support of people who will tell you the truth in love.
Grace does not excuse what destroys us.
Grace teaches us to turn away from it.
Titus 2:11–12 says that the grace of God teaches believers to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts and to live soberly, righteously, and godly.
That is one of the most beautiful and challenging truths of the Gospel.
Jesus does not merely forgive us so that we can remain comfortable in the darkness.
He saves us to bring us into the light.
And sometimes coming into the light hurts.
It hurts to admit that the person you have blamed for years is not responsible for every decision you have made.
It hurts to acknowledge that the addiction you keep defending is enslaving you.
It hurts to confess that your religious appearance has become more important to you than your private obedience.
It hurts to admit that you have been asking God to bless a life you have refused to surrender to Him.
But there is mercy in that exposure.
Because the Savior who calls you to repentance is the same Savior who stretched out His arms on the cross for sinners.
Remember Adam in the garden.
He hid among the trees.
And God called to him.
Now remember Jesus at Calvary.
He was nailed to a tree.
And through His sacrifice, guilty sinners can be reconciled to God.
In Eden, human beings grasped at what God had forbidden.
At Calvary, the obedient Son submitted to the Father's will.
In Eden, shame led humanity into hiding.
Through Christ, forgiven sinners are invited to approach God with confidence.
In Eden, sin brought death into the human story.
Through the risen Christ, eternal life is promised to all who believe in Him.
Paul draws the great comparison between Adam and Christ in Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15.
Through Adam came sin and death.
Through Christ come righteousness, resurrection, and life for those who belong to Him.
The Bible is not a collection of disconnected moral lessons.
It is the unfolding story of God's holiness, humanity's rebellion, and His saving purpose fulfilled in Jesus Christ.
From the garden to the cross.
From the cross to the empty tomb.
From the empty tomb to the promised restoration of all things.
And in Revelation 22, the Bible's closing vision brings us back to the imagery of life, the tree of life, and the removal of the curse.
What humanity lost through rebellion cannot be recovered by human effort.
But God has acted in Christ to bring His people into the life they could never earn.
That is why our message at Gospel Warrior is more than a memorable phrase.
Not because Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
Not because consequences always disappear.
Not because every earthly story receives the ending we wanted.
But because Christ can redeem sinners, reconcile them to God, transform their lives, and give them a future that sin and death cannot finally destroy.
Think about Peter.
He promised that he would never abandon Jesus.
Then, under pressure, he denied knowing Him three times.
Imagine the sound of the rooster.
Imagine Peter remembering the words of Jesus.
Imagine the unbearable realization that his courage had collapsed when it mattered most.
Luke 22:62 tells us that Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Yet the risen Jesus did not leave Peter's story at that courtyard.
In John 21, Jesus restored Peter and called him again to serve.
Peter's denial was real.
His grief was real.
His restoration was real.
And the grace of Christ was greater than his failure.
Perhaps you needed to remember that today.
Not because your failure is unimportant.
But because your failure is not more powerful than the Savior.
Peter could not undo his denial.
But Jesus could restore him.
The thief on the cross could not go back and live a different life.
But Jesus could promise him paradise (Luke 23:43).
Paul could not erase his history of persecuting Christians.
But the risen Christ could show him mercy and transform him into a servant of the Gospel (1 Timothy 1:12–16).
And you cannot travel backward through time to undo every word, every choice, or every betrayal.
But you can turn to the Savior who died and rose again.
You can repent.
You can believe.
You can begin walking in obedience today.
You can seek reconciliation where possible.
You can tell the truth.
You can stop hiding behind religious language and finally bring your actual heart before God.
And if you have already placed your faith in Jesus, you can remember that your standing before God rests on Christ, not on your ability to maintain the appearance of perfection.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus…” (KJV)
That promise is not a license to cherish sin.
It is freedom from condemnation for those who belong to Christ.
And when believers stumble, 1 John 1:9 calls them to confess their sins, trusting God's faithfulness and righteousness to forgive and cleanse.
Maybe the enemy has been reminding you of everything you used to be.
But the Gospel invites you to remember who Jesus is.
The serpent is not your savior.
Your shame is not your judge.
Your past is not your redeemer.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
And His resurrection is not dependent on whether you feel victorious this morning.
He is risen whether your hands are trembling.
He is risen whether your prayers come through tears.
He is risen whether your healing takes longer than you expected.
He is risen whether the people who wounded you ever apologize.
And because He lives, those who trust in Him have a living hope.
There is something deeply personal about this.
Somewhere, someone is reading these words while sitting beside a hospital bed.
Someone is reading while wondering how to pay the next bill.
Someone is reading after a night of fighting temptation.
Someone is reading with a Bible open and tears falling onto the pages.
Someone is reading after being told that their life will never amount to anything.
And someone is reading who has not prayed sincerely in years.
If that someone is you, please understand what the promise in Genesis 3:15 is ultimately pointing toward.
Not a secret technique for making every problem disappear.
Not a guarantee that faithful Christians will never suffer.
Not a declaration that you can defeat the devil through your own strength.
It points toward Jesus Christ, the promised Redeemer, whose death and resurrection have decisively confronted sin, death, and the devil.
And He calls you to Himself.
Not to an image you have carefully constructed.
Not to a religious performance.
To Himself.
Jesus said:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” (Matthew 11:28, KJV)
That invitation is still beautiful.
Still urgent.
Still true.
If you have never trusted Christ, do not confuse admiration for Jesus with surrender to Jesus.
The Gospel calls us to repent and believe (Mark 1:15).
Acknowledge your sin before God.
Stop treating His mercy as something you can earn.
Trust in the crucified and risen Savior.
And follow Him.
If you are a believer who has wandered, do not make peace with the darkness.
Come back into the light.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Seek help where help is needed.
Return to Scripture.
Return to prayer.
Return to fellowship with faithful believers.
And remember that the One who began a good work in His people is faithful to carry it forward (Philippians 1:6).
Perhaps you need words to begin.
You can pray something like this, not as a formula that earns salvation, but as an honest expression of repentance and faith:

“Lord Jesus, I have sinned against You. I have tried to hide what You already know. I cannot save myself, and I cannot undo my past. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising from the dead. I turn away from my sin and place my trust in You. Forgive me, change my heart, teach me to obey You, and help me walk in Your truth. I belong to You. Amen.”
And if that prayer reflects the sincere cry of your heart, do not keep your journey isolated.
Find a faithful, Bible-teaching local church.
Seek baptism and discipleship.
Open the Scriptures.
Learn to follow Jesus in ordinary, costly, beautiful obedience.
Because the Christian life is not only about the moment you first believe.
It is about a lifetime of being shaped by the grace and truth of Christ.
And that brings me to something I want to ask you personally.
If this message has uncovered a battle you have been fighting in silence, would you be willing to speak honestly?
You do not need to reveal private details or expose wounds you are not ready to share.
Or, if you are struggling to hold on:
“I'm still fighting.”
And if you need prayer:
“Pray for me.”
Not because a comment saves you.
Not because public confession is a substitute for repentance before God.
But because someone else reading may be convinced that they are the only person who is struggling.
Your few words might remind them that they are not alone, and that hope is found in Jesus Christ.
Not to glorify the past.
But to glorify the Savior.
There may also be someone on your Facebook friends list who needs this message.
Someone who used to be active in church but has quietly disappeared.
Someone who keeps posting that everything is fine while privately falling apart.
Someone in your family who has been carrying guilt for years.
Someone who does not yet know Christ.
Not as another piece of content to fill a feed.
But as a way of placing the truth of Scripture where someone might encounter it at the right moment.
Send it privately to someone who needs compassion more than public attention.
Invite your family, your friends, believers who need strengthening, those who have grown spiritually cold, and those who are still seeking answers to follow as well.
We are building a community that wants more than momentary inspiration.
We want to know Christ more deeply.
To understand His Word faithfully.
To repent sincerely.
To love one another.
And to grow into mature disciples who can stand firm when life becomes difficult.
These resources are intended to help people grow deeper in Scripture, strengthen their faith, and develop a more Christ-centered life.
And if this ministry has been a blessing to you, I want to invite you to consider something beyond reading, liking, or sharing.
For some, supporting Gospel ministry financially is a meaningful expression of generosity and worship.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should come from a willing heart, not from pressure or compulsion.
And that matters deeply to us.
You are not purchasing God's favor.
You are not paying for grace.
You are helping make freely accessible Gospel resources possible for others.
The deeper purpose is to help this ministry continue reaching people with the truth of Jesus Christ.
Read.
Learn.
Pray.
Invite others.
Use the free resources.
Your financial circumstances do not determine your worth before God, and the Gospel must never become something only paying supporters can access.
Our prayer is that every resource, every article, every testimony, and every act of support would ultimately direct attention away from ourselves and toward Jesus Christ.
Because He is the reason this message exists.
He is the promised offspring.
He is the obedient Son.
He is the crucified Savior.
He is the risen King.
He is the One who will bring the serpent's defeat to its final fulfillment.
And when we return to Genesis 3:15, something becomes impossible to ignore.
God announced the promise while Adam and Eve were still standing in the wreckage of their disobedience.
They had no achievements to offer.
No righteousness of their own to present.
No way to restore Eden by human strength.
Yet the Lord revealed that evil would not have the final word.
That is the wonder of redemption.
The first human scandal did not defeat God's saving purpose.
The cross did not defeat His Son.
The tomb did not hold Him.
And the final future of those who belong to Jesus is not determined by the serpent's accusations, but by the victory of the Lamb.
So the next time shame tells you to hide, remember the garden.
The next time suffering makes you question whether God has abandoned you, remember the cross.
The next time death seems stronger than hope, remember the empty tomb.
And the next time the enemy whispers that your story is already over, remember the promise God spoke at the beginning.
The serpent struck the heel.
But Jesus Christ rose from the dead.
And the serpent's final defeat is certain.
The wound was real. The blood was real. The grave was real. But so was the resurrection—and the serpent never gets to write the ending.
